claims.text: Conventional solidification or homogenization produces a predominantly single-phase HEA with coarse grains.
High rolling reduction followed by controlled annealing can induce an ultrafine, lamellar dual-phase microstructure in an HEA.
The proposed processing will generate abundant nano-twins and coherent interphase boundaries.
Closely spaced interphase boundaries and refined lamellae impede dislocation motion and increase strength.
The hierarchical dual-phase microstructure impedes crack propagation.
Hierarchical microstructural obstacles promote uniform strain partitioning.
Dislocation obstruction and sustained work hardening increase strength.
The refined hierarchical microstructure maintains ductility by delaying shear localization.
Improved load distribution at coherent interfaces enhances Young's modulus.
Crack deflection at coherent interfaces enhances fracture resistance.
The treatment will improve yield strength by approximately 20–50% relative to conventionally processed controls.
The treatment will maintain or improve ductility while increasing strength.
The treatment will produce a balanced or enhanced Young's modulus.
The treatment will enhance fracture toughness.
Optimizing deformation, annealing, and cooling parameters can favor controlled phase separation and microstructural refinement.
The approach may fail in alloys that form brittle intermetallic phases or have diffusion too slow for the required microstructural evolution.
Excessive grain growth, unwanted coarse phases, or poor processing control can prevent the predicted improvements.
The magnitude of improvement and the strength–ductility balance will vary with alloy chemistry and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance will all be enhanced simultaneously, whereas the predicted outcome only requires ductility to be maintained and describes Young's modulus merely as balanced.

The predicted outcome permits maintained ductility and does not quantify a required modulus or toughness increase, but the falsification rule appears to require statistically significant improvements in all four properties.
